extracted.intended_audience: mathematical-olympiad students and advanced high-school/early-university problem-solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of olympiad-style problems and worked solutions in algebra and geometry (inequalities, induction, roots/coefficients, rearrangements, basic geometry and loci). Focus is on methods and classical results used to solve contest problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convexity (definition / Jensen-type inequality)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f convex on I and 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1, f(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y). Similar inequalities for concave functions with reversed sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout to compare values of f at convex combinations. Example uses: proving f(a−b+c) ≤ f(a) − f(b) + f(c) by representing points as convex combinations and adding inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twice-differentiable convexity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is twice differentiable, then f is convex on I iff f''(x) ≥ 0 on I (and concave iff f''(x) ≤ 0 on I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute f'' to check convexity (used to justify applying Jensen/convexity arguments; e.g., f(x)=x/(s−x) has f''>0 on (0,s), hence convex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection inequality for convex functions (Problem 1.71)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is convex on interval I and a < b < c in I, then f(a − b + c) ≤ f(a) − f(b) + f(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: write b as convex combination of a and c, get f(b) ≤ λf(a)+(1−λ)f(c), write a−b+c as other convex combination and add inequalities. Generalizes to alternating sums for odd-length sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using convexity to prove symmetric rational inequalities (Problem 1.72)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a/(b+c)+b/(a+c)+c/(a+b) ≥ 3/2, set s=a+b+c and consider f(x)=x/(s−x), note f''(x)=2s/(s−x)^3 > 0, so f is convex and apply Jensen/convexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: rewrite symmetric expression in terms of a single-parameter convex function and apply Jensen or convexity averaging f(a)+f(b)+f(c) ≥ 3 f(s/3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral inequalities via convexity and translation (Problem 1.73)
rubrics_metrics.description: For convex integrable f on [1,13],  ∫_1^3 f + ∫_{11}^{13} f ≥ ∫_5^9 f. (Derivation uses pointwise inequality f(a+6)+f(a+4) ≤ f(a)+f(a+10) for convex f and integrates over a.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: obtain discrete convexity inequalities by choosing appropriate translates, then integrate over parameter to get inequalities between integrals on different intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction: prove stronger statements when needed (section 1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: When plain induction fails because the RHS is fixed but LHS increases, prove a stronger statement (e.g. add a corrective −1/n term) that is stable under the inductive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated in Problem 1.81: to bound a product by 3, show a stronger inequality 1+1/n^3 ≤ 3 − 1/n to allow inductive step. General advice: strengthen the induction hypothesis to make step n→n+1 feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of binomial theorem + induction for divisibility (Fermat's little theorem, Problem 1.82)
rubrics_metrics.description: For prime p and integer a, show p | (a^p − a) by induction using (a+1)^p expansion and the fact that binomial coefficients C(p,k) divisible by p for 1 ≤ k ≤ p−1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine induction hypothesis with divisibility of intermediate binomial coefficients; standard combinatorial number-theory induction technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: AM–GM inequality (Problem 1.76)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple proofs exist: rearrangement-based proof and classical algebraic proofs; used extensively to bound arithmetic sums by geometric means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating-sum inequality for convex functions (generalization of Problem 1.71)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows by iterating the two-point inequality used in Problem 1.71; reversed for concave f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viète's relations (roots ↔ coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: For polynomial P(X)=a0 + a1 X + ... + an X^n with roots x1,...,xn, x1+...+xn = −a_{n−1}/a_n, sum of products of roots etc. (classical Viète equalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to translate symmetric conditions on roots to coefficient relations and vice versa; useful for deducing algebraic structure of roots (e.g., geometric progression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factoring via Viète to detect structure of roots (example Problem 1.92)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given relations among symmetric sums (e.g. (ab+bc+ca)^3 = abc(a+b+c)^3), use Viète to express in terms of polynomial coefficients, factor and deduce properties of roots (e.g., two roots multiply to a square ratio ⇒ geometric sequence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: introduce monic polynomial with given roots, write Viète equalities, manipulate/factor polynomials to extract root relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement inequality (section 1.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For ordered sequences x1 ≤ x2 ≤ ... ≤ xn and y1 ≤ y2 ≤ ... ≤ yn, among all permutations σ, S(σ)=Σ xi y_{σ(i)} is maximal when σ is identity (same order) and minimal when σ is reversed (opposite order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by swapping inversions; equality cases discussed (ties allow multiple optima). Used to derive many classical inequalities like AM–GM, Cauchy–Schwarz, and various symmetric bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observations on ordering (ties/monotone non-strict sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: If sequences satisfy x1 ≤ x2 ≤ ... ≤ xn and y1 ≤ y2 ≤ ... ≤ yn (non-strict), conclusion of rearrangement still holds though maxima/minima may not be unique (e.g., all xi equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful when equal elements occur — multiple permutations may attain extrema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: quadratic-form extremum (Problem 1.103/observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For real xi, x1^2+...+xn^2 ≥ x1 x_{σ(1)} + ... + xn x_{σ(n)} for any permutation σ (special case of rearrangement with same sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consequence of arranging both sequences identically to maximize dot product; used to prove inequalities like Σ x_i^2 ≥ Σ x_i x_{σ(i)}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rearrangement to prove a^3+b^3+c^3 ≥ 3abc (Problem 1.104)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange sequences appropriately (a,b,c and a^2,b^2,c^2) and apply rearrangement twice to reach inequality chain ending with 3abc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates rearrangement applicability beyond linear sums; useful for symmetric homogeneous inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving AM–GM and Cauchy–Schwarz via rearrangement (Problems 1.105 & 1.106)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct auxiliary sequences (products scaled by geometric mean) and apply rearrangement to obtain AM–GM; use normalized sequences and doubling trick to obtain Cauchy–Schwarz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives alternative proofs illustrating how ordering arguments can yield classical inequalities; helpful for contest solution variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chebyshev's inequality (Problem 1.112)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a1 ≤ ... ≤ an and b1 ≤ ... ≤ bn (both ordered), then (average of a)·(average of b) ≤ average of products: ((Σ a_i)/n)((Σ b_i)/n) ≤ (Σ a_i b_i)/n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be proved from rearrangement by summing appropriate inequalities; useful when sequences have same monotonicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality and equality condition (section 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any three points A,B,C, AC + BC ≥ AB with equality iff C lies on segment AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic geometric tool used in many proofs; equality characterization important for extremal geometry problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint-segment equality in quadrilateral (Problem 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: In convex quadrilateral with M,N midpoints of AD and BC, MN = (AB + CD)/2 iff AB ∥ CD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: compare MN with half-sums of parallels to diagonals and apply triangle inequality; equality when mid-segment aligns with parallels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus for equal triangle areas via medians and parallels (section 2.2 & Problem 2.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locus of points M with [ABM] = [ACM] (in triangle ABC) is the median AD. More generally, for quadrilateral ABCD (AB not parallel to CD), locus of M with [ABM] = [CDM] is the segment of the median of triangle T X Y (T intersection of AB and CD) inside the quadrilateral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: translate segments to share common vertex T and reduce area-equality to condition that M lies on a median of triangle formed by translated segments; locus may be a segment or line depending on configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus for linear combinations of areas (Problem 2.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locus of M with [ABM] + [CDM] = k reduces (via translations) to requirement that [XMY] be constant, hence M lies on a line parallel to XY; depending on k the locus inside quadrilateral is a segment, point or empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform area-sum to area of triangle with fixed base, so locus is line(s) parallel to fixed line; check intersection with polygon interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for cyclic quadrilateral (section 2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A convex quadrilateral is cyclic iff sum of opposite angles equals 180°. Equivalent condition: angle between one side and a diagonal equals angle between opposite side and the other diagonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these criteria to detect cyclicity; many constructions/proofs (incenters forming rectangle, orthocenters relationships) depend on cyclicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incenters of triangles in a cyclic quadrilateral form a rectangle (Problem 2.29)
rubrics_metrics.description: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, incenters of triangles ABC, BCD, CDA, DAB are vertices of a rectangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses equalities of certain angle expressions derived from cyclicity, shows successive angles of the incenter-quadrilateral are right angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equiangular polygon distance-sum property (Problem 2.39)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a convex equiangular polygon, for any point P in interior or on sides, the sum of distances from P to the polygon's sides is constant (independent of P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For regular polygon proof: area = (1/2)*side_length*sum(distances). For general equiangular polygon, expand to a regular polygon to add constant offsets. Converse holds for triangles (constant sum ⇒ equilateral) but not for quadrilaterals (parallelogram counterexample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex-root-of-unity criterion for side-lengths of equiangular polygon (Problem 2.40)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an equiangular n-gon has side lengths a1,...,an in counterclockwise order and ε = exp(2π i / n), then a1 + a2 ε + a3 ε^2 + ... + an ε^{n−1} = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret sides as vectors and sum to zero; conversely, given positive ai satisfying that complex sum equals zero, an equiangular polygon with those side lengths exists (but converse not fully equivalent in general).
